newsitem.title: CHINA: Airbus wants to accelerate China 100-seat plane.
newsitem.headline: Airbus wants to accelerate China 100-seat plane.

text.p: European consortium Airbus Industrie sees its priority in China in 1997 as accelerating a joint venture to produce 100-seat airliners, the China Daily Business Weekly said on Sunday/

"The AE-100 project is one of the most important issues in 1997 and the one that is significant to our long-term strategy," the newspaper quoted Jean Pierson, Airbus president and managing director, as saying during a recent visit to Beijing.
Airbus was also eager to create customer service training centres in China this year, he said.

The three sides in the 100-seater airliner venture would sign a final contract in May before launching the project, and this would include agreement on the product, engineering, manufacturing and marketing organisation and cost sharing.

In June 1996, Aviation Industries of China (AVIC), Aero International Asia (AIA), under the European consortium Aero International (Regional), and Singapore Technologies Aerospace signed a contract to develop the 100-seater.
AVIC will play the lead role in the project. Airbus joined the venture to replace Aero International after restructuring last year.
"To make our product family cover the series from 100 to more than 600 seats, we consider the AE-100 project of strategic importance to Airbus," Pierson said.
He said 60 percent of the demand for 100-seat planes was in Europe and the United States, so it was necessary to set up a powerful marketing group to make the AE-100 compatible with the Airbus fleet.

Customer service training centres near Beijing's Capital Airport and established by China Aviation Supplies Corp and Airbus Industrie, were expected to be open full-time in the third quarter, he said.

Consisting of a training centre for pilots and mechanics, a spare parts service centre and a repair centre, they are the first combined training and customer support facilities in China with investment of $100 million, he said.

Pierson said 15 European and U.S. parts suppliers had agreed to set up facilities at the support centre to provide on-site technical training, repairs and service for Chinese operators of Airbus aircraft.
By the end of the year, all Airbus parts suppliers are expected to be represented at the centre, he said.
In 1997, Airbus will deliver 26 planes to Chinese customers, including Hong Kong and Macau, bringing the number of Airbus aircraft in China to more than 80, the newspaper said.
